'''Chaudhry Abdul Majeed''' (born 1937; {{langx|ur|چودہری عبد لمجيد}}) was a Pakistani [[nuclear chemist]], [[nuclear weapon]] and [[nuclear reactor technology|reactor]] expert. He is known as one of the pioneers of Pakistan's [[Pakistan and weapons of mass destruction|nuclear weapon programme]], and has worked closely with former [[Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission]] (PAEC) Chairman [[Munir Ahmad Khan]]'s [[Pakistan Atomic Research Reactor#PARR-III Reactor (New-Labs)|plutonium reprocessing project]]. He rose to prominence when he was apprehended by Pakistan's intelligence agencies in a joint operation in late October 2001. Majeed was also one of the founding members of [[Sultan Bashiruddin Mahmood]]'s [[Ummah Tameer-e-Nau]] organisation; an NGO which caused an international embarrassment for Pakistan.

==Education==
Majeed was educated in [[Lahore]], [[Punjab (Pakistan)|Punjab]], British Indian Empire. In 1955, he attended [[University of Engineering and Technology, Lahore|University of Engineering and Technology]] of Lahore, and took a double [[Bachelor of Science]] (BSc) in mathematics and chemistry in 1959. The same year, he was admitted to the High-Tension Laboratory, a physics department for advanced courses in Nuclear sciences, at the [[Government College University, Lahore|Government College University]], where he gained his [[Master of Science]] (MSc) in [[nuclear chemistry]].

In 1964, Majeed went to Belgium on a [[scholarship]] awarded by PAEC and attended [[Katholieke Universiteit Leuven]], from which he received his [[Doctor of Science]] (D.Sc.) in Nuclear Chemistry in 1968. He continued his academic research at the [[plutonium]] facility in Belgium in the late 1960s.<ref name="The Hindu">
{{Cite news
  | last = Bidwai
  | first = Praful
  | title = Nuclear chickens come home
  | newspaper = The Hindu
  | location = [[Chennai]], [[Tamil Nadu]], India
  | pages = 49/55
  | date = 10 November 2001
  | url = http://www.hinduonnet.com/fline/fl1823/18230180.htm
  | access-date = 6 March 2010
  | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20051223050126/http://www.hinduonnet.com/fline/fl1823/18230180.htm
  | archive-date = 23 December 2005
  | url-status = usurped
  }}
</ref> Majeed received training at the [[Nuclear Plant Tihange|''Tihange'']] and [[Nuclear Plant Doel|''Doel'']] nuclear facilities in Belgium.<ref name="The Hindu"/> As a senior scientist he had access to classified documentation on sensitive plutonium technology which is critical to develop a nuclear weapon.<ref name="The Hindu"/> Majeed also worked at the [[International Center for Theoretical Physics]] (ICTP) invited by [[Abdus Salam]], during the 1970s and early 1980s. At ICTP, Majeed taught advanced courses in chemistry and mathematics, and published numerous research papers in the field of [[spectroscopy]], [[neutron detection|neutron]] and [[particle detector]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Albright |first=David |author-link=David Albright |author2=Holly Higgins |title=A Bomb for Ummah: The Others |date=April 2003 |url=https://people.reed.edu/~ahm/Courses/Stan-PS-314-2009-Q1_PNP/Syllabus/EReadings/AlbrightHiggins2003A-Bomb.pdf }}{{dead link|date=November 2016 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

==Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission==
Majeed returned to Pakistan in 1974 after India had conducted a surprise nuclear test, codenamed "[[Pokhran-I]]". At the [[Pakistan Institute of Nuclear Science and Technology]] (PINSTECH) he was assigned to the Nuclear Chemistry Division led by [[Iqbal Hussain Qureshi]]. In 1974, Majeed was a part of [[Munir Ahmad Khan]]'s team that had supervised the [[Critical mass|criticality]] of the second nuclear pile —[[Pakistan Atomic Research Reactor#PARR-II Reactor|PARR-II]] reactor.<ref name="Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists"/> After the construction of the third nuclear pile—[[Pakistan Atomic Research Reactor#PARR-III Reactor (New-Labs)|PARR-III]], also known as The New-Labs; Majeed was the first [[technical director]], and was part of a team that supervised the reactor's criticality.<ref name="Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists"/> An expert in plutonium technology, Majeed, as junior scientist, is known for his contribution in the plutonium [[Nuclear reprocessing|reprocessing]] plant and plutonium [[nuclear fuel cycle]] technology.<ref name="Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists"/> Majeed was also a part of a team at the New Labs that had succeeded in attaining fresh supplies of [[weapons-grade plutonium]] isotopes, produced by the reactor.<ref name="Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists"/> In 1990, Majeed was promoted and was made Director-general of Nuclear Chemistry Division (NCD) by Munir Ahmad Khan.<ref name="Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists">{{Cite web
  | last =Albright
  | first = David
  |author2=Holly Higgins
  | title = Pakistani Nuclear Scientists: How Much Nuclear Assistance to Al Qaeda?
  | website = Institute for Science and International Security
  | publisher = Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists
  | date =30 August 2002
  | url = http://www.exportcontrols.org/pakscientists.html
  | access-date = 6 March 2010}}
</ref> Throughout the 1990s, Majeed was responsible for underground work of the nuclear reactor ''[[Khushab-I]]'', and the [[Chashma Nuclear Power Plant|''CHASNUPP-I'']] commercial nuclear power plant.<ref name="Institute for Science and International Security"/> There, he was the director of Radiation and Nuclear Safety Division and was omitted from the weapons development teams.

He published extensively in the 1980s and 1990s on nuclear detectors and the use of [[x-ray diffraction]], [[fluorescence]], and [[crystallography]] to study a wide variety of materials and elements, including stainless steel, [[uranium]], [[plutonium]], and [[thorium]].<ref name="Institute for Science and International Security">{{Cite web
  | last =Albright 
  | first =David
  | author-link =David Albright 
  |author2=Holly Higgins 
  | title =Pakistani Nuclear Scientists:Who is Majeed 
  | website =[[Institute for Science and International Security]] 
  | publisher =Institute for Science and International Security 
  | date =30 August 2002
  | url =http://www.exportcontrols.org/pakscientists.html 
  | access-date = 6 March 2010}}</ref> Due to his work for the State, he was conferred with the [[Tamgha-e-Imtiaz]] awarded by the [[Prime Minister of Pakistan]], [[Nawaz Sharif]], in 1998.<ref name="Institute for Science and International Security"/>

==Events of 2001==

He was one of the founding members of a Pakistani militant organisation called [[Ummah Tameer-e-Nau]]. He was accused of travelling through [[Afghanistan]] without notifying the [[Government of Pakistan]]. Along with fellow nuclear scientist [[Sultan Bashiruddin Mahmood]], he was arrested in October 2001 in Islamabad by a joint-operation of the [[Inter-Services Intelligence]] and the [[Federal Investigation Agency]], because of their connections to the [[Taliban]].<ref name="The Hindu" />

In the hope of securing a quick release from the intelligence agencies and returning to his research at the [[Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission|PAEC]], he readily confessed. The [[FIA]] and [[Inter-Services Intelligence|ISI]]'s joint-Intelligence report, which was given to the [[Parliament of Pakistan|Parliament]]'s Committee on National Security and Defence Affairs, stated that Majeed admitted that [[Osama bin Laden]] had asked them to build either a [[Radiological weapon|radiological]] or a [[Biological warfare|biological weapon]].<ref name="Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists" /> He was subsequently designated by the [[Al-Qaida and Taliban Sanctions Committee]] of the [[Security Council]] in December 2001.<ref>{{Cite web |title=AQ Sanctions List |url=https://www.un.org/securitycouncil/sanctions/1267/aq_sanctions_list |publisher=[[United Nations]]}}</ref>

The first interrogation of the two [[Pakistani people|Pakistani]] [[scientist]]s concluded that Mahmood and Majeed did not know enough to help build a nuclear weapon. "These two guys were nuclear scientists who didn't know how to build one themselves," the American official said. "If you had to have guys go bad, these are the guys you'd want. They didn't know much."<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/11/28/world/nation-challenged-biological-terror-2-pakistanis-linked-papers-anthrax-weapons.html?pagewanted=all | title=A Nation Challenged: Biological terror; 2 Pakistanis Linked to Papers on Anthrax Weapons | work=The New York Times | date=28 November 2001 | access-date=24 July 2012 |author1=Frantz, Douglas  |author2=Rohde, David}}</ref>

==Aftermath and legacy==

He was harshly interrogated for a long time, which also resulted in his death. Bashir Syed, former President of the Association of Pakistani Scientists and Engineers of North America (APSENA), said: "I know both of these persons and can tell you there is not an iota of truth that both these respected scientists and friends will do anything to harm the interest of their own country."<ref name=nature>{{cite journal|last=Adam|first=David|title=Atomic-bomb experts interrogated over Taliban links|journal=Nature|date=1 November 2001|volume=414|issue=3|pages=3|doi=10.1038/35102221|bibcode = 2001Natur.414....3A|pmid=11689900|doi-access=free}}</ref>
